title: Solo dev, full-time job, no budget: a year of writing my space RTS by hand, then eight weeks with an AI coding agent. Here's what changed.
author: dmarshallgaming
selftext:
I'm a solo dev with a full-time job and a tiny budget. Cosmic Dominion is a 2D space game where you fly your own flagship in every fight while running a real-time war for a galaxy, against AI commanders who play by the same rules you do. The free demo went out on Steam and [itch.io](http://itch.io) on October 29.

I started it the normal way, writing every line myself in Unity/C#, in the evenings. After about a year I had 121 scripts, \~16K lines and 18 tests. Then the day job won and it barely moved for most of this year.

In September I started working with Claude Code (an AI coding agent that works directly in the repo). Eight weeks later:

* 977 commits (vs about 180 in the year before)
* \~225K lines of C# across 920 files
* \~2,700 automated tests
* a guided tutorial, a 10-mission campaign plus endless scenarios, 13 factions with their own traits, sieges and boarding parties, an insectoid swarm, save/load, a full settings menu, controller and Steam Deck support, Steam leaderboards and a WebGL build

**What the AI does:** most of the code, the tests, the editor tools that build the UI, and a lot of the debugging.

**What I still do:** decide what the game is, play it constantly, and say what's wrong. Most of the work is me playing, writing down what felt bad ("the alarm is too easy to ignore", "I can't tell when a planet gets breached"), and the agent tracing it back through the code. Eleven outside playtesters so far, in person and through Provenance, and every session turned into a list of fixes, usually within a day or two. One said flying the ship was the hardest part for a new player and suggested an autopilot; the next day you could ALT+right-click a planet and the ship flies itself there while you shoot.

Things that made it work:

* **Make it measure, not guess.** The game has a headless "autoplay" mode that plays whole AI-vs-AI games at 45x speed and writes stats. Balance changes get tested over dozens of seeded games before I play them. Runs are reproducible per seed, so an A/B means something.
* **Tests for every rule.** The game logic lives in small pure classes with unit tests, so the agent can change one thing without quietly breaking three others.
* **Write down the why.** The repo has a long design doc of every decision and the playtest that caused it. The agent reads it before touching a system, which stopped it from undoing old fixes.
* **Playtest anyway.** Tests catch logic bugs, not "this feels bad." Nothing replaces watching someone else play.

Art: the ships, effects and UI are licensed asset packs, the planet sprites are AI-generated, and the audio is licensed. It's all disclosed on the Steam page.

Happy to answer anything about the workflow: what went wrong, how I keep it from breaking things, how I review it.
